title: Journal of Experimental Psychology: General - Vol 155, Iss 10

items.title: From stigma to trust: A paradigm shift for understanding perceptions of individuals with bipolar disorder.
items.content: Individuals with bipolar disorder (BD) face professional and personal challenges such as underemployment. Navigating these challenges involves the dilemma of whether to disclose their illness or conceal it and risk presenting symptoms. Examinations of these challenges are often anchored in stigma, which has attributed negative employment outcomes for individuals with BD to adverse reactions from managers following disclosure. Across three experiments, including a managerial sample and a novel chatbot interaction, and eight supplemental studies (N = 8,112), the present research proposes and tests a trust-based attributional model. Mania, the hallmark symptom of BD, signals activation-based unpredictability, which serially erodes the perceived trustworthiness of an employee, ultimately compromising a manager’s trust and willingness to retain the employee. The current findings demonstrate that disclosure is not uniformly harmful and that stigma operates as a distal moderator. An employee disclosing in the absence of mania can appear less predictable, and managers high in preexisting stigma toward BD generally view employees as less predictable. However, when manic symptoms are visible, disclosure buffers against their negative impact by providing an explanation for the erratic behavior. Together, this research reveals that moving beyond stigma-centric accounts clarifies managerial perceptions of employees with BD, with disclosure and stigma shaping this trust-based process. items.title: “A girl is the champion!”: Well-intentioned gendered messages can backfire.
items.content: Initiatives aimed at promoting gender equity in majority-male domains often emphasize gender to highlight women’s achievements (e.g., “Space4Women,” “all-women spacewalk”). Does such gendered messaging help achieve equity goals? Two theoretical accounts offer competing predictions. An informational account suggests that referencing a gender alongside a domain should strengthen beliefs that the referenced gender participates and succeeds. A pragmatic account, however, predicts that explicitly marking gender may backfire by signaling that the referenced gender is atypical in the domain—otherwise, why mention it? We tested these two possibilities with U.S. children (ages 4–10; N = 326) and adults (N = 788). Participants learned about fictional activities described with either gendered messaging (e.g., “A girl/boy is the Gazzer champion”) or control messaging (e.g., “Joan/Rob is the Gazzer champion”). Gendered messaging backfired compared to control messaging on average, causing participants to infer lower participation by the referenced gender and, among adults, lower ability. Gendered messaging also undermined participants’ interest in the activities. A meta-analysis across experiments revealed small-to-moderate effects that were larger for adults than children, consistent with developmental changes in pragmatic reasoning. Finally, backfire effects disappeared for messaging about fictional groups, suggesting that background knowledge about the referenced group may be needed to trigger pragmatic inferences. Together, these findings advance theoretical accounts of pragmatic reasoning while indicating that well-intentioned gendered messaging may paradoxically undermine equity goals. A more effective alternative may be to clearly feature women in a domain without explicitly framing it as being “for them.” (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

items.title: Individual differences in motor and auditory activation in second language speech learning: Roles of domain-general auditory processing.
items.content: While existing models emphasize the critical roles of auditory and motor systems in speech perception, it remains unclear how individual learners differentially rely on these systems and how their relative weighting relates to language learning. This study investigates the neural mechanisms through which individual differences in domain-general auditory processing influence reliance on these networks during second language (L2) phonetic learning. Focusing on the acquisition of English [æ] and [ʌ] by 207 Japanese learners, we examined participants with varying auditory precision profiles using both behavioral and functional magnetic resonance imaging analyses as they performed discrimination tasks for speech and nonverbal sounds. The findings revealed a pattern consistent with a triangular relationship among learners’ auditory precision, brain activation in motor-related regions, and L2 speech development. Learners with lower auditory precision tended to show less advanced L2 vowel proficiency and exhibited higher levels of sensorimotor activation during discrimination of English [æ] and [ʌ], but not during discrimination of nonspeech counterparts with comparable second formant variation. In light of theoretical accounts of adult L2 speech learning (Best & Tyler, 2007), one possible interpretation is that greater reliance on articulatory processing among less auditory-precise and less experienced or proficient L2 learners reflects the processing of L2 sounds through first language articulatory routines. In contrast, learners with higher auditory precision attained not only more advanced L2 vowel proficiency but also lower levels of sensorimotor activity, comparable to that observed during nonverbal processing, suggesting more balanced spectrotemporal and articulatory analyses of sounds, which optimize both the process and outcomes of L2 speech learning. items.title: Naturally disengaging control to reveal habits.
items.content: Habits are an essential part of everyday decision making, yet the mechanisms underlying human habit formation and expression are difficult to study in laboratory settings, where participants typically engage strong goal-directed (GD) control that can mask habitual tendencies. Recent approaches have successfully elicited habits in long experiments by limiting the amount of GD control participants can exert (e.g., through forced response times). We extend this approach by designing a short behavioral paradigm that aims to induce and reveal habits without extrinsically limiting GD control, instead incorporating task features that we hypothesized would encourage participants to spontaneously relax GD control: a hierarchical multistep trial structure, opportunities for self-correction, and frequent switches between extensively and minimally practiced behaviors. Across seven experiments, we demonstrate that this approach induces habitual control in a relatively brief paradigm. Specifically, overtraining increases slips of action toward the extensively practiced context and reduces slips toward the minimally practiced one, indicating behavioral inflexibility at early response times, while slower responses remain dominated by GD control. Systematic manipulation of task features across experiments revealed that allowing multiple response attempts was particularly important for reliably observing this overtraining effect; a hierarchical trial structure may further facilitate habit expression, though this remains inconclusive. More broadly, our paradigm provides a practical tool for investigating how habits form and interact with goal-directed control. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)
